title: Using the GitHub Actions Toolkit
learning_outcomes: Explain the key behavior of using the github actions toolkit and identify when it should be used.
Configure or review the workflow fields and permissions relevant to using the github actions toolkit.
Verify the result using a controlled run or static check and interpret the evidence.

content.intro: This lesson focuses on using the github actions toolkit. The Actions Toolkit offers helpers for reading inputs, setting outputs, logging annotations, and reporting failures consistently from a JavaScript action. Use the example to predict the workflow result, then verify the behavior in a safe test repository or by static review.
content.why_it_matters: Using the GitHub Actions Toolkit matters because it affects correctness, security, maintainability, or operating cost. content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: The Actions Toolkit offers helpers for reading inputs, setting outputs, logging annotations, and reporting failures consistently from a JavaScript action. Reuse the right abstraction: reusable workflows compose jobs; composite actions bundle steps; JavaScript or container actions package executable behavior. Define inputs, outputs, permissions, and versions explicitly. The most useful check is one that produces observable evidence and fails clearly when its stated requirement is not met.

items.title: Core toolkit functions
items.text: For core toolkit functions, state the expected input and result, identify the relevant workflow field or operational decision, and verify it with a controlled check plus run logs. Document the failure condition rather than relying on the YAML file merely parsing.

items.title: Input and output handling
items.text: Write one step output as `name=value` to `$GITHUB_OUTPUT`, then declare job outputs if a downstream job needs the value. Use `$GITHUB_ENV` for values needed by later steps in the same job.

items.title: Logging and annotations
items.text: Start with the first failed step and its exit code, then inspect the event, conditions, permissions, tool versions, network, and runner state. Capture sanitized diagnostics and preserve evidence of the failure.

items.title: Failure reporting

items.title: Debug messages

items.title: State and workflow command integration
items.text: Make the workflow contract explicit: identify the event, job runner, inputs, command/action, output, and failure signal. Keep steps small and review the permissions and source of every action.

content_blocks.code:
name: Validate custom action
on: [push, pull_request]
permissions:
  contents: read
jobs:
  test-action:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Install action dependencies
        run: npm ci
      - name: Run action tests
        run: npm test
content_blocks.expected_output: The workflow tests the action repository with its lockfile; adapt the commands to the action’s implementation and test framework.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Run in the custom action repository after confirming its package scripts and dependencies.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Keep action tests separate from publication credentials.

content_blocks.title: Practice and verification
content_blocks.text: Inspect the example and make one focused change related to using the github actions toolkit. Predict the expected result first, then use the run instructions or a static review to check it. Record the difference between your prediction and the actual result. Do not add production secrets or grant write permissions just to make a sample pass.

items.title: Syntax and scope
items.text: Check YAML indentation and confirm whether the setting belongs at workflow, job, or step level.

items.title: Permissions and trust
items.text: Start with read-only access. If the example needs more access, explain the exact operation and reduce permissions again afterwards.

items.title: Evidence
items.text: Use the run summary and first failing step. A green result is meaningful only when the intended checks actually ran.

content_blocks.title: Recap
content_blocks.text: You should now be able to explain using the github actions toolkit, read the example, and identify a way to validate it. The wider system goal remains: Package shared workflow logic behind clear input/output contracts and maintained versions.

content.task: Apply using the github actions toolkit to a small workflow change. State the expected result first, validate the configuration, then record evidence from the run or static check.
task_acceptance_criteria: Identify the relevant event, workflow field, runner behavior, or security boundary.
Explain the expected success result and at least one failure or skip condition.
Use least privilege and a disposable/test context; do not include credentials or production resources.
hints: Start with the key behavior: The Actions Toolkit offers helpers for reading inputs, setting outputs, logging annotations, and reporting failures consistently from a JavaScript action.
Inspect the exact event filters, permissions, expressions, inputs, and job dependencies that affect this example.
Compare the observed status and logs with the expected result; distinguish static validation from a real hosted run.
content.expected_output: The expected result is the behavior described here: The Actions Toolkit offers helpers for reading inputs, setting outputs, logging annotations, and reporting failures consistently from a JavaScript action. The real result depends on the repository, selected ref, configured permissions, and runner availability.
troubleshooting: If a workflow never starts, verify the workflow is under `.github/workflows/`, the event and filters match, and repository/organization Actions policy allows it.
If a step fails, inspect the first failed step, exit code, stderr, installed tool versions, permissions, and runner/network state before retrying.
If a job is skipped or data is missing, inspect `if`, `needs`, outputs, artifact names/paths, and cache keys; jobs do not automatically share filesystems.
common_mistakes: Assuming YAML parsing proves the workflow runs correctly or matches the intended trigger.
Granting broad token permissions, printing environment values, or exposing a secret to untrusted code.
Using a placeholder command as evidence of a real build, test, deployment, or security scan.
summary: The Actions Toolkit offers helpers for reading inputs, setting outputs, logging annotations, and reporting failures consistently from a JavaScript action.

Reuse the right abstraction: reusable workflows compose jobs; composite actions bundle steps; JavaScript or container actions package executable behavior. Define inputs, outputs, permissions, and versions explicitly.
Use the provided example as a starting point, replace placeholders with repository-specific checks, and validate both success and expected failure behavior before publication.
